title: ICP - NOC Nanopore Tree of Life Metabarcoding - analysis report
text:
This project evaluates the use of Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing combined with a Tree of Life metabarcoding approach for broad-scale marine biodiversity assessment. Environmental DNA (eDNA) samples were collected using the RoCSI autonomous sampling system and subsequently analysed using the portable MinION sequencing platform, providing a workflow that combines autonomous marine sampling with rapid, portable molecular analysis.




The NOC’s Robotic Cartridge Sampling Instrument (RoCSI).





The Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencing device.



The study uses 33 seawater samples collected during the BIO-Carbon II cruise aboard the RRS James Cook, along a transect extending from northern Scotland to Cardiff and covering much of the west coast of Great Britain. The transect spans contrasting marine environments and substantial gradients in environmental conditions, including temperature, salinity and chlorophyll concentration, providing a valuable test bed for assessing the ability of ONT metabarcoding to characterise biodiversity across different marine habitats.





By integrating portable nanopore sequencing with autonomous eDNA sampling, the project also contributes to the development of faster and more scalable approaches to marine biodiversity monitoring. Ultimately, such workflows could support the transition from conventional retrospective eDNA analysis towards near-real-time biodiversity observations at sea.


Before looking into the metabarcoding data, let’s have a quick look at the metadata.

text:
Bioinformatics processing parameters
Primer trimming was performed with Cutadapt v5.2, followed by ASV inference and taxonomic assignment using DADA2.
For all markers, Cutadapt used an error rate of 0.1, minimum primer overlap of 15 bp, no indels and --discard-untrimmed. Both forward and reverse primer matches were required.

DADA2 settings shared across markers:

Filtering: maxEE = c(2,3), maxN = 0, minLen = 200, rm.phix = TRUE.
Denoising: Independent forward/reverse error models, with pool = "pseudo".
Paired-end merging: minOverlap = 90, trimOverhang = TRUE.
Chimera removal: method = "consensus", allowOneOff = FALSE.
Taxonomy: assignTaxonomy() using marker-specific reference databases; 16S species-level assignment additionally used addSpecies().

Truncation lengths are expressed as R1/R2 in base pairs. “None” indicates no fixed-length truncation. Other unspecified settings used DADA2 defaults.

data_dir <- "data/Illumina"
markers <- c("16S", "18S", "COI", "MiFish", "ITS", "rbcL")

for (m in markers) {
  track <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, paste0(m, "_read-count-tracking.rds")))
  seqtab <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, paste0(m, "_seqtab_nochim.rds")))
  taxa   <- readRDS(file.path(data_dir, paste0(m, "_taxa.rds")))

  assign(paste0("track_", m), track)
  assign(paste0("seqtab_", m), seqtab)
  assign(paste0("taxa_", m), taxa)

Code
qc_samples <- map_dfr(markers, function(m) {

  track <- get(paste0("track_", m))
  seqtab <- get(paste0("seqtab_", m))

  # Check sample matching
  stopifnot(setequal(rownames(track), rownames(seqtab)))

  # Match tracking rows to ASV table rows
  track <- track[rownames(seqtab), , drop = FALSE]

  tibble(
    marker = m,
    sample = rownames(seqtab),
    input_reads = track[, "dada2_input"],
    filtered_reads = track[, "filtered"],
    merged_reads = track[, "merged"],
    final_reads = track[, "nonchim"],
    retention = track[, "final_perc_reads_retained"],
    n_ASVs = rowSums(seqtab > 0),
    sample_type = case_when(
      str_detect(sample, "Extract-ctrl$") ~ "Extraction control",
      str_detect(sample, "NTC$") ~ "PCR control",
      TRUE ~ "Biological"
    )
  )
})




Code
# 1. Combine DADA2 tracking data -----------------------------------------

qc_tracking <- purrr::map_dfr(markers, function(m) {

  get(paste0("track_", m)) %>%
    as.data.frame() %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("sample") %>%
    mutate(
      marker = m,
      sample_type = case_when(
        str_detect(sample, "Extract-ctrl$") ~ "Extraction control",
        str_detect(sample, "NTC$") ~ "PCR control",
        TRUE ~ "Biological"
      )
    )
})

# 2. Calculate median reads at each processing step -----------------------

qc_steps <- qc_tracking %>%
  filter(sample_type == "Biological") %>%
  group_by(marker) %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      c(dada2_input, filtered, dada_f, merged, nonchim),
      median
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -marker,
    names_to = "step",
    values_to = "median_reads"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    step = factor(
      step,
      levels = c("dada2_input", "filtered", "dada_f",
                 "merged", "nonchim")
    )
  )

# 3. Figure: DADA2 read retention ----------------------------------------

p_retention <- ggplot(
  qc_steps,
  aes(x = step, y = median_reads, group = 1)
) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2", size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ marker, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c(
    dada2_input = "Input",
    filtered = "Filtered",
    dada_f = "Denoised F",
    merged = "Merged",
    nonchim = "Nonchim"
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Median reads per sample",
    title = "DADA2 read retention across markers",
    subtitle = "Biological samples only"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1)
  )

print(p_retention)

# 4. Figure: Final sequencing depth per sample ----------------------------

p_depth <- qc_samples %>%
  mutate(
    marker = factor(marker, levels = markers),
    sample_type = factor(
      sample_type,
      levels = c("Biological", "Extraction control", "PCR control")
    ),
    sample_order = as.integer(str_extract(sample, "^[0-9]+"))
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    x = sample_order,
    y = final_reads,
    fill = sample_type
  )) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~ marker, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Biological" = "#0072B2",
    "Extraction control" = "#D55E00",
    "PCR control" = "#CC79A7"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 10, 20, 30, 34, 35)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Sample number",
    y = "Non-chimeric reads",
    fill = NULL,
    title = "Final sequencing depth per sample"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

Code
library(tidyverse)
library(vegan)

markers <- c("16S", "18S", "COI", "MiFish", "ITS", "rbcL")

# Calculate rarefaction curves -------------------------------------------

rarefaction <- purrr::map_dfr(markers, function(m) {

  seqtab <- get(paste0("seqtab_", m))

  # Exclude both negative controls
  seqtab <- seqtab[
    !grepl("Extract-ctrl$|NTC$", rownames(seqtab)),
    , drop = FALSE
  ]

  # Remove zero-depth samples
  seqtab <- seqtab[rowSums(seqtab) > 0, , drop = FALSE]

  # Depths covering the full range of each sample
  max_depth <- max(rowSums(seqtab))
  depths <- unique(round(seq(1, max_depth, length.out = 60)))

  purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(seqtab)), function(i) {

    sample_depth <- rowSums(seqtab[i, , drop = FALSE])

    d <- unique(c(
      depths[depths <= sample_depth],
      sample_depth
    ))

    tibble(
      marker = m,
      sample = rownames(seqtab)[i],
      depth = d,
      richness = vapply(
        d,
        function(n) as.numeric(
          vegan::rarefy(seqtab[i, , drop = FALSE], sample = n)
        ),
        numeric(1)
      )
    )
  })
})

# Summary curves:
# Recalculate on a common depth grid for each marker so that
# all biological samples contribute at every plotted depth.

rarefaction_summary <- purrr::map_dfr(markers, function(m) {

  x <- get(paste0("seqtab_", m))

  # Exclude negative controls
  x <- x[!grepl("Extract-ctrl$|NTC$", rownames(x)), , drop = FALSE]

  # Exclude COI sample 22
  if (m == "COI") {
    x <- x[!grepl("^22_COI_", rownames(x)), , drop = FALSE]
  }

  depths <- unique(round(seq(1, min(rowSums(x)), length.out = 60)))

  purrr::map_dfr(depths, function(d) {

    richness <- as.numeric(vegan::rarefy(x, sample = d))

    tibble(
      marker = m,
      depth = d,
      mean_richness = mean(richness),
      sd_richness = sd(richness)
    )
  })
})

# Combined figure --------------------------------------------------------

p_rarefaction_combined <- ggplot(
  rarefaction_summary,
  aes(x = depth, y = mean_richness, colour = marker, fill = marker)
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      ymin = pmax(0, mean_richness - sd_richness),
      ymax = mean_richness + sd_richness
    ),
    alpha = 0.15,
    colour = NA
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(
    x = "Sequencing depth (reads)",
    y = "Expected ASV richness",
    colour = "Marker",
    fill = "Marker",
    title = "Rarefaction curves across markers",
    subtitle = "Mean ± SD across biological samples"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

unclassified_summary <- purrr::map_dfr(markers, function(m) {

  ps <- get(paste0("ps_", m))

  tax_df <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"))

  tax_df %>%
    summarise(across(
      everything(),
      ~ sum(
        is.na(.) |
        trimws(as.character(.)) == "" |
        tolower(trimws(as.character(.))) == "unclassified"
      )
    )) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      everything(),
      names_to = "Rank",
      values_to = "n_unclassified_ASVs"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      Marker = m,
      total_ASVs = ntaxa(ps),
      percent_unclassified = 100 * n_unclassified_ASVs / total_ASVs
    )
})

library(tidyverse)
library(phyloseq)

markers <- c("16S", "18S", "COI", "MiFish", "ITS", "rbcL")

# Define a general taxonomic order spanning all databases
rank_levels <- c(
  "Empire",
  "Domain",
  "Kingdom",
  "Supergroup",
  "Division",
  "Subdivision",
  "Subkingdom",
  "Phylum",
  "Subphylum",
  "Class",
  "Order",
  "Family",
  "Genus",
  "Species"
)

# Count assigned ASVs at each rank for each marker
assigned_summary <- purrr::map_dfr(markers, function(m) {
  
  ps <- get(paste0("ps_", m))
  tax_df <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(ps), "matrix"))
  
  tibble(
    Rank = colnames(tax_df),
    n_assigned_ASVs = sapply(tax_df, function(x) {
      sum(
        !is.na(x) &
        trimws(as.character(x)) != "" &
        !tolower(trimws(as.character(x))) %in% c("na", "unclassified")
      )
    }),
    Marker = m,
    total_ASVs = ntaxa(ps)
  )
})

# Keep only ranks that are actually present
assigned_summary <- assigned_summary %>%
  mutate(
    Rank = factor(Rank, levels = rank_levels),
    Marker = factor(Marker, levels = markers)
  ) %>%
  arrange(Marker, Rank)

# Combined plot
p_assigned_combined <- ggplot(
  assigned_summary,
  aes(x = Rank, y = n_assigned_ASVs, colour = Marker, group = Marker)
) +

my_colors <- c(
  "#FF6666", "#8DD3C7", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A",
  "#984EA3", "#A6D854", "#FFFF33", "#FF7F00",
  "#F781BF", "#999999", "#66C2A5", "#FC8D62",
  "#8DA0CB", "#E78AC3", "#FFD92F", "#E5C494",
  "#B3B3B3", "#A65628", "#FFFFB3", "#BEBADA",
  "#FB8072", "#80B1D3", "#FDB462"
)

plot_class_composition <- function(ps, marker, top_n = 20) {

  # 1. Keep biological samples only
  ps <- subset_samples(ps, SampleType == "Biological")
  ps <- prune_samples(sample_sums(ps) > 0, ps)
  ps <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(ps) > 0, ps)

  # 2. Replace missing class assignments
  tax <- as(tax_table(ps), "matrix")

  tax[, "Class"][
    is.na(tax[, "Class"]) |
    trimws(tax[, "Class"]) == "" |
    tolower(trimws(tax[, "Class"])) %in% c("na", "unclassified")
  ] <- "Unassigned"

  tax_table(ps) <- tax_table(tax)

  # 3. Agglomerate to Class
  ps_class <- tax_glom(
    ps,
    taxrank = "Class",
    NArm = FALSE
  )

  # 4. Convert to relative abundance
  ps_rel <- microbiome::transform(
    ps_class,
    "compositional"
  )

  # 5. Select top classes by mean relative abundance
  top_classes <- microbiome::top_taxa(
    ps_rel,
    n = top_n
  )

  # 6. Melt and group remaining classes
  df <- psmelt(ps_rel) %>%
    mutate(
      Class = as.character(Class),
      Class_plot = if_else(
        OTU %in% top_classes | Class == "Unassigned",
        Class,
        "Other"
      ),
      Number = as.integer(
        stringr::str_extract(Sample, "^[0-9]+")
      )
    ) %>%
    group_by(Sample, Number, Class_plot) %>%
    summarise(
      Abundance = sum(Abundance),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  # 7. Order classes by total relative abundance
  class_order <- df %>%
    filter(!Class_plot %in% c("Other", "Unassigned")) %>%
    group_by(Class_plot) %>%
    summarise(
      Total = sum(Abundance),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(Total)) %>%
    pull(Class_plot)

  class_order <- c(
    class_order,
    intersect("Unassigned", unique(df$Class_plot)),
    intersect("Other", unique(df$Class_plot))
  )

  df$Class_plot <- factor(
    df$Class_plot,
    levels = class_order
  )

  # 8. Assign colours
  plot_colors <- setNames(
    rep(my_colors, length.out = length(class_order)),
    class_order
  )

  if ("Unassigned" %in% class_order) {
    plot_colors["Unassigned"] <- "#666666"
  }

  if ("Other" %in% class_order) {
    plot_colors["Other"] <- "#C0C0C0"
  }

  # 9. Plot
  ggplot(
    df,
    aes(
      x = factor(Number, levels = 1:33),
      y = Abundance,
      fill = Class_plot
    )
  ) +
    geom_col(width = 0.85) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = plot_colors,
      drop = FALSE
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      labels = scales::percent,
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
    ) +
    labs(
      title = paste0(marker, " — Class-level composition"),
      x = "Sample number",
      y = "Relative abundance (%)",
      fill = "Class"
    ) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      axis.text.x = element_text(
        angle = 45,
        hjust = 1
      ),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.direction = "horizontal"
    ) +
    guides(
      fill = guide_legend(nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE)
    )
}

text:
Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) metabarcoding data were processed for multiple marine eDNA markers, including 16S, 18S V4, ITS, COI and MiFish 12S. The workflow was developed iteratively using representative samples before being applied across the full dataset.
The general processing strategy consisted of:

Identifying and removing PCR primers using Cutadapt and retaining only reads containing the expected linked forward and reverse primer combination. Applying marker-specific length filters.
Applying read-quality filtering using Chopper.
OTU consensus generation using Amplicon_sorter.
Assigning taxonomy using DADA2 assignTaxonomy()

For each marker, Cutadapt was supplied with the expected primer pair in both orientations using linked adapters:
cutadapt \
    -g FORWARD...REVERSE_COMPLEMENT_REVERSE \
    -g REVERSE...REVERSE_COMPLEMENT_FORWARD \
    --error-rate <marker-specific> \
    -O 15 \
    --cores=0 \
    --discard-untrimmed

library(tidyverse)

Consensus sequences generated independently for each sample using amplicon_sorter were combined into a single FASTA file. Sequences were dereplicated using VSEARCH (--derep_fulllength --strand both) to retain unique sequences at 100% identity, accounting for reverse complements. This reduced 6,791 consensus sequences to 2,118 unique sequence variants (OTUs).
Original primer-trimmed and quality-filtered Nanopore reads were mapped against these OTUs using Minimap2 (map-ont). Primary alignments were extracted, excluding secondary, supplementary and unmapped alignments. Reads were retained if they met the following criteria:

Alignment identity ≥95%
Query coverage ≥95%
No minimum mapping quality (MAPQ) threshold

Read counts per OTU were aggregated across all 33 samples and two controls to generate the OTU abundance table.
Results: A total of 4,340,358 reads were assigned to 2,118 OTUs across 35 samples and controls. Of these, 1,703 OTUs received at least one read, while 415 had zero assigned reads. The latter may reflect ambiguous mapping between closely related sequence variants or alignment filtering and require further investigation.
Outputs: otu_table.tsv, otu_representatives_final.fasta and mapping_qc.tsv.






NoteZero-abundance OTUs



Of the 2,118 unique consensus variants, 1,703 recruited at least one read after filtering, while 415 (19.6%) had zero assigned reads. Among the latter, 333 (80.2%) received primary alignments that failed the ≥95% identity and/or coverage criteria, 81 (19.5%) received only secondary alignments, and one (0.2%) received no alignments.
These results indicate that zero-abundance variants primarily resulted from alignment filtering and competition among closely related consensus sequences rather than complete failure of read recruitment.
Importantly, each retained sequencing read was counted only once, using its primary Minimap2 alignment. Overall, 4,340,358 reads (97.3% of input reads) were assigned to OTUs. Although closely related variants may compete for read assignments, this uncertainty may be reduced by aggregating abundances at higher taxonomic ranks following taxonomic classification.


The OTU count table (otu_table.tsv) and representative sequences (otu_representatives_final.fasta) were imported into R and saved as otu.rds. Taxonomy was assigned using DADA2 assignTaxonomy() and addSpecies() against SILVA v138.2, generating taxa.rds and taxa_bootstrap.rds.
Taxonomic assignment was successful for 99.8% of reads at phylum level, 84.8% at family level, 70.7% at genus level and 3.1% at species level. The OTU table, taxonomy and representative sequences were then combined into a phyloseq object for downstream analyses.

COI recovered the highest number of unique sequence variants (3,079), followed by 16S (2,118) and 18S (1,918). COI also produced the greatest number of assigned reads (8.81 million), reflecting differences in sequencing depth and potentially amplification efficiency among markers.
Following read mapping and filtering (≥95% identity and coverage), 11.8–19.6% of unique consensus variants received no reads. This proportion was highest for 16S (19.6%) and lowest for COI (11.8%). Zero-abundance OTUs likely result from alignment filtering and competition among closely related consensus variants, as demonstrated for 16S.
Overall, the workflow successfully generated read-abundance tables for all three markers while preserving single-nucleotide differences between consensus sequences. However, differences in OTU richness should not be interpreted directly as differences in biological diversity without accounting for marker-specific resolution, amplification biases and sequencing depth.

Combining all three databases increased the number of genus-classified OTUs to 542 (17.6%), leaving 2,537 OTUs (82.4%) unclassified.

Agreement was highest between eKOI and MZG (60.9%). MIDORI2 showed substantially lower agreement, including implausible metazoan assignments for sequences classified as marine protists by the other databases.



Three OTUs (215 reads; 0.0024% of all COI reads) were classified as vertebrates. eKOI identified two closely related OTUs as Homo sapiens (200 reads) and one as Ovis aries (15 reads). These identifications were supported by independent BLASTn searches, including a 100% identity match across the full amplicon for O. aries. In contrast, MZG assigned these sequences to fish taxa, with low genus-level bootstrap support.
These mammalian sequences may represent low-level contamination, although their occurrence across samples and negative controls should be examined before drawing conclusions.



eKOI and MZG provided the most useful and complementary COI classifications, increasing genus-level coverage from 399 to 530 OTUs when combined. MIDORI2 contributed limited additional coverage and showed substantial taxonomic disagreement. Overall, the low genus-level classification success highlights limitations in available COI reference databases and the importance of independent validation of uncertain taxonomic assignments.



The MIDORI2 UNIQ COI reference database (3,213,682 sequences) was processed to extract the region targeted by the mlCOIintF/jgHCO2198 primers for taxonomic assignment of nanopore metabarcoding data.
An initial Cutadapt approach requiring detection of both primers retained only 258,463 sequences (8.0%), substantially reducing reference coverage. Further investigation showed that many references contained the forward-primer region but lacked a detectable reverse-primer binding site, probably because sequences had been truncated during their original preparation.
The extraction strategy was therefore revised:

Forward-primer trimming: Cutadapt (-e 0.25, minimum overlap 24 bp, no indels) retained 2,960,095 sequences (92.1%).
Reverse-primer trimming: The reverse-complemented jgHCO2198 primer was removed when detected (-e 0.30, minimum overlap 20 bp, no indels), while unmatched references were retained. Primer-match positions were examined to identify appropriate matching parameters.
Length optimisation: Sequences exceeding 330 bp were truncated, preserving natural length variation among shorter references.
Minimum-length filtering: References shorter than 100 bp were excluded to remove fragments with limited taxonomic information.

The resulting database is expected to contain 2,948,559 sequences (91.8% of the original), approximately 11.4 times more references than the initial two-primer extraction. This strategy substantially improves potential taxonomic coverage while restricting reference sequences to the targeted COI region.
The impact on taxonomic assignment accuracy and computational performance remains to be evaluated.



The MIDORI2 COI database was processed to retain the target amplicon region while maximising reference coverage, resulting in 2.95 million sequences (100–330 bp), representing 91.8% of the original database.
Taxonomic assignment using DADA2’s assignTaxonomy() performed unexpectedly poorly. Of 3,079 COI OTUs, 2,622 were assigned to Arthropoda, with no assignments beyond class level. Many assignments were clearly incorrect, including algal, cnidarian and vertebrate OTUs classified as Arthropoda with high bootstrap confidence.
To investigate this, six representative OTUs were analysed using VSEARCH. All had biologically consistent best matches in MIDORI2 (84.7–100% identity), including exact matches for Phaeocystis globosa and Arachnanthus sarsi. When DADA2 was retrained using a small reference subset containing these matches, all six OTUs were correctly classified at phylum level with 92–100% bootstrap confidence.
These results demonstrate that MIDORI2 contains suitable reference sequences, but DADA2 performs unreliably with the complete training database. Reference redundancy, taxonomic representation and heterogeneous reference lengths may contribute, although the precise cause remains unresolved.
We therefore decided to adopt VSEARCH-based taxonomic assignment, which provides explicit nucleotide identity, alignment coverage and access to competing reference matches. This approach allows more transparent assessment of taxonomic confidence and ambiguity, particularly for high-quality nanopore consensus sequences.



Since I used the same SILVA reference and DADA2 taxonomy functions for my Illumina 16S data, I could compare the two sequencing technologies using: - Percentage of OTUs/ASVs classified at each rank. - Percentage of sequencing reads classified at each rank. - Genus-level bootstrap confidence distributions.
